t: #2344 Minimum Deletions to Make Array Divisible — Editorial
o:
After deletions, the SMALLEST remaining element of nums must divide every element of numsDivide. Key observation: x divides all of numsDivide iff x divides g = gcd(numsDivide). Also any such divisor x satisfies x ≤ g. So the only viable candidates are elements of nums that are ≤ g and divide g.

Strategy: sort nums ascending; walk from the smallest, deleting (counting) every element that does not divide g; the first element dividing g gives the answer = number skipped. If none, return -1.

Example 1: g = gcd(9,6,9,3,15) = 3; deleting the two 2s leaves min 3 | 3 → answer 2. Example 2: g = 2; 4 and 3 don't divide 2 and 6 > 2 → -1.
k: x divides all of numsDivide ⇔ x divides gcd(numsDivide).
Any valid minimum is ≤ g, so scanning nums in ascending order, the first element dividing g is optimal.
Answer = count of elements before that first valid element; -1 if no element divides g.

a.i: Reduce numsDivide to its gcd g in one pass, sort nums, and scan upward counting deletions until hitting a divisor of g.
s: Compute g = gcd of all numsDivide.
Return the index of the first element with g % element == 0, or -1.
a.t: O(D + N log N) — one gcd pass over numsDivide plus sorting nums.

w: The gcd reduction collapses the problem instantly; without it you'd waste time testing each candidate against the whole numsDivide. Pitfalls: forgetting that equal small elements each count as separate deletions (index i already accounts for duplicates), and testing divisibility the wrong direction (need g % x == 0, not x % g). Follow-up: what if you had to make the LARGEST element divide everything — symmetric reasoning with lcm-style bounds.
